1.note: Jeremiah is using **thus says Yahweh** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.
See how you translated this phrase in 40:11.

1.q: הֲ⁠בָנִ֥ים אֵין֙ לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אִם יוֹרֵ֖שׁ אֵ֣ין ל֑⁠וֹ
1.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that Israel does have sons and heirs who should possess the land of Gad. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Israel certainly has sons! He certainly has an heir!]

1.q: מַדּ֗וּעַ יָרַ֤שׁ מַלְכָּ⁠ם֙ אֶת גָּ֔ד וְ⁠עַמּ֖⁠וֹ בְּ⁠עָרָ֥י⁠ו יָשָֽׁב
1.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the Ammonites for taking land that did not belong to them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is wrong that their king has taken possession of Gad and that his people dwell in his cities!]

This could mean: (1) **their king** refers to the king of Ammon, who took the territory of the tribe of Gad. (2) **their king** refers to Milcom, the god of the Ammonites, whose name sounds like the word for “king” in the original language. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the Ammonite king]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:3.

2.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because Ammon has done this]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [listen carefully]
See how you translated **days are coming** in 7:32.
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8.

2.q: וְ֠⁠הִשְׁמַעְתִּי אֶל רַבַּ֨ת בְּנֵי עַמּ֜וֹן תְּרוּעַ֣ת מִלְחָמָ֗ה
2.note: Here, **the shout of war** represents the attack of an enemy army, whose soldiers shout their battle cry as they attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [when I will cause an enemy army to attack Rabbah of the sons of Ammon]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a mound that is completely deserted]

The expression **her daughters will be kindled with fire** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, it is the enemy soldiers who will attack Rabbah. Alternate translation: [and enemy soldiers will set her daughters on fire]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the villages around Rabbah as if they were Rabbah’s **daughters**. It means that these villages depended on Rabbah in the way that daughters depend on their mother. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the villages that depend on her will be kindled with fire]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:3.
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:5.

3.note: Yahweh is speaking to **Heshbon**, a city that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the destruction that is coming on Ammon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people of Heshbon. Alternate translation: [Wail, you who live in Heshbon]

The expression **Ai has been devastated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, it is the enemy army. Alternate translation: [the enemy army has devastated Ai]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh is speaking of the villages around Rabbah as if they were the **daughters** of Rabbah, since they depended on Rabbah as daughters depend on their mother. (2) the phrase **daughters of Rabbah** refers to the women of Rabbah. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [towns near Rabbah]

This could mean: (1) the people will run back and forth **among the walls** of their city or fields because they are terrified. (2) the word translated **walls** refers to the stone walls of sheepfolds, and the people will run back and forth among the sheepfolds. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and run to and fro in terror among the walls of your city]
The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Ammon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for the king of the Ammonites will go into exile]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his priests and his officials will go into exile together]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:8.

4.note: The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Ammon as if they were one woman. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people of Ammon for boasting about their valleys. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have no reason to boast in the valleys]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the valley of Ammon were **flowing** with water. It means that the valley is very fertile and produces abundant crops. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your valley producing abundant crops]
See how you translated this phrase in 31:22.

Even though Yahweh is addressing the people of Ammon directly, he is speaking of them in the third person as **the one trusting in her treasures**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [you who trust in your treasures]

The people of Ammon are using the question form to boast that no one would dare to attack them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one will come against me!]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that no one will come against her]

5.note: Yahweh is using **Behold me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to act]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [causing you to be terrified]

The expression **you will be scattered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, it is the enemies who will attack Ammon. Alternate translation: [And your enemies will scatter you]

Yahweh is using **a man to his face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each person straight ahead.” It describes people running away in panic without stopping to help anyone else. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every person fleeing in panic on his own]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **one fleeing**. He means any of the people of Ammon who flee. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and there will be no one gathering any of those who flee]
See how you translated this name in 2:19.

6.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the punishment he has just described and the restoration he will bring on the people of Ammon afterward. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, after I have punished them]
See how you translated this expression in 29:14.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8.

7.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that there is no longer any wisdom in Teman. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no longer any wisdom in Teman!]
The word **Teman** is the name of a region in Edom.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if **Counsel** were a living thing that has **perished**. It means that the discerning people of Edom are no longer able to give wise advice. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The discerning ones are no longer able to give good advice]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **wisdom** of the Edomites were fruit that has **rotted away**. It means that their wisdom has become useless. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their wisdom has become useless]
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:3.
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:3.

8.note: Yahweh is using **Make deep to dwell** as a common expression of the culture to mean “hide yourselves in deep places.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Hide yourselves in deep places]
The word **Dedan** is the name of a region southeast of Edom.

Here, **Esau** represents the Edomites, who were the descendants of Esau. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the calamity of Edom]

Yahweh is using **visit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time I punish him]

9.q: אִם בֹּֽצְרִים֙ בָּ֣אוּ לָ֔⁠ךְ לֹ֥א יַשְׁאִ֖רוּ עֽוֹלֵל֑וֹת
9.note: The implication is that, even though **grape gatherers** and **thieves** always leave something behind, Yahweh will leave nothing at all for the Edomites. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Others always leave something behind, but I will leave you nothing at all. If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings]

The word **If** introduces a hypothetical situation. Yahweh is describing what would happen if **grape gatherers came** to Edom in order to contrast it with what he himself will do to Edom. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Even if grape gatherers were to come to you]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that grape gatherers always leave some grapes behind. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [they would certainly leave gleanings!]

10.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Edom, whom he calls **Esau**, as if they were a person whom he would **strip** of all his clothing. It means that he will allow their enemies to take away everything they own. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will let enemies take away everything that the people of Edom own]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would **uncover** the places where Esau hides. It means that he will expose every place where the Edomites might try to hide, so that they will have nowhere to escape. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will find every place where he tries to hide]
See how you translated “seed” in 7:15 where it is used with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [His descendants are devastated]

Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between grape gatherers and thieves, who leave some things behind, and himself, who will leave nothing for Esau. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But unlike them]

The expression **His seed is devastated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, it is Yahweh, who will use enemy soldiers to destroy Edom. Alternate translation: [I will devastate his seed]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his brothers are devastated and his neighbors are devastated]

Yahweh is using **he is no more** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will no longer exist.” Here **he** refers to Esau, meaning the people of Edom. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the people of Edom will no longer exist]
See how you translated “seed” in 7:15 where it is used with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [His descendants are devastated]

11.note: The word **your** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Edom as if they were one man. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The implication is that the men of Edom will be killed and will leave behind their children and their wives, and that Yahweh himself will take care of them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you die, leave your children who have no father to me]

Yahweh is using the adjective **fatherless** as a noun to mean children whose fathers have died. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your children whose fathers have died]

12.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Take note that]

12.q: אֲשֶׁר אֵ֨ין מִשְׁפָּטָ֜⁠ם לִ⁠שְׁתּ֤וֹת הַ⁠כּוֹס֙ שָׁת֣וֹ יִשְׁתּ֔וּ
12.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of his punishment as if it were a **cup** of wine that people must **drink**. It means that even people who did not deserve to be punished will certainly suffer punishment. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who did not deserve punishment will certainly receive it]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the Edomites will certainly not escape punishment. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you will certainly not be the one who goes free!]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb translated **acquitting** and **acquitted** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [without question, will be acquitted]

The expression **You will not be acquitted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [I will not acquit you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 24:8.
See how you translated the similar expression in 25:28.

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 22:5.
The word **Bozrah** is the name of a city. It was one of the main cities of Edom.

The terms **a horror**, **a reproach**, **a desolation**, and **a curse** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the four terms together to emphasize how completely Bozrah will be ruined and disgraced. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [utterly ruined and disgraced]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **ruins** that are characterized by **perpetuity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [permanent ruins]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8.
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:15.

14.note: The implication is that the speaker has changed from Yahweh to Jeremiah, who is now telling what he heard from Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Jeremiah, have heard a report from Yahweh]

The expression **an envoy has been sent** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh has sent an envoy among the nations]
The pronoun **her** refers to Edom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and come against Edom]

The people sending the message are using **rise up for the battle** as a common expression of the culture to mean “get ready to fight.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and prepare yourselves to fight]

15.q: כִּֽי הִנֵּ֥ה קָטֹ֛ן נְתַתִּ֖י⁠ךָ בַּ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם בָּז֖וּי בָּ⁠אָדָֽם
15.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [For behold, I will make you utterly despised among the nations]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [indeed]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would make the Edomites **small** in size. It means that he will make them weak and unimportant among the other nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make you weak among the nations]

The expression **despised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who will do the action, it is the people of other nations. Alternate translation: [and mankind will despise you]

Here the masculine term **mankind** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [among people]

16.note: Yahweh is speaking of **Your terror** as if it were a living thing that could deceive the Edomites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have deceived yourself by trusting in the terror you cause others]

This could mean: (1) **Your terror** refers to the terror that the Edomites caused in other people. The implication is that because other nations were afraid of them, the Edomites wrongly thought that they were safe. (2) **Your terror** refers to the dread that the Edomites themselves feel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The fear that other nations have of you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Edomites’ pride were located in their **heart**, which represents a person’s thoughts and feelings. It means that the Edomites were very proud. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your great pride]

Even though Yahweh is addressing the Edomites directly, he is speaking of them in the third person as **one dwelling in the clefts of the rock**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [you who dwell in the clefts of the rock]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Edomites were **grasping** the hilltops with their hands. It means that they occupy the high places and hold on to them firmly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [occupying and firmly holding the height of the hill]

Yahweh uses the word **Though** here to indicate a contrast between the high places where the Edomites live and his ability to bring them down from there. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Even if you make your nest high like the eagle]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the eagle** builds its nest high in places that are hard to reach, so the Edomites build their homes high in the rocky cliffs where they think that no one can reach them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [you build your homes high in places that are hard to reach, as the eagle builds its nest]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would physically **bring** the Edomites **down** from a high place. It means that he will humble them and defeat them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will still humble you and defeat you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8.

17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 19:8.

Hissing was a symbolic action by which people showed that they were shocked by what had happened to someone and that they scorned that person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and will hiss in shock and scorn over all of her wounds]
See how you translated this phrase in 19:8.
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:16.

18.q: כְּֽ⁠מַהְפֵּכַ֞ת סְדֹ֧ם וַ⁠עֲמֹרָ֛ה וּ⁠שְׁכֵנֶ֖י⁠הָ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה לֹֽא יֵשֵׁ֥ב שָׁם֙ אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹֽא יָג֥וּר בָּ֖⁠הּ בֶּן אָדָֽם
18.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [“Like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and her neighbors,” says Yahweh, “absolutely no person will dwell in her at all]

18.q: כְּֽ⁠מַהְפֵּכַ֞ת סְדֹ֧ם וַ⁠עֲמֹרָ֛ה וּ⁠שְׁכֵנֶ֖י⁠הָ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה
18.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who is speaking, **says Yahweh**, before the comparison **Like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and her neighbors**. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that, like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and her neighbors]

The point of this comparison is that just as **Sodom and Gomorrah and her neighbors** were completely destroyed so that no one lived there anymore, so Edom will be completely destroyed and no one will live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Edom will be completely destroyed, just as Sodom and Gomorrah and her neighbors were overthrown]

The implication is that Yahweh had completely destroyed **Sodom and Gomorrah** long ago because their people were very wicked. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Like the complete overthrow long ago of wicked Sodom and Gomorrah]
The pronoun **her** refers to Sodom and Gomorrah together, not to Edom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the neighbors of Sodom and Gomorrah]

18.q: לֹֽא יֵשֵׁ֥ב שָׁם֙ אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹֽא יָג֥וּר בָּ֖⁠הּ בֶּן אָדָֽם
18.note: Here the masculine terms **man** and **son of man** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [no person will dwell there, and a human being will not sojourn in her]

Yahweh is using **a son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a human being.” Here it means “anyone.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a single person]
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:3.

19.q: וּ⁠מִי זֶ֣ה רֹעֶ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר יַעֲמֹ֖ד לְ⁠פָנָֽ⁠י
19.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no ruler can resist him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And there is no shepherd who can stand before my face!]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a continual stream]

Here, **pastureland** represents the “sheep” that would graze in the pastureland. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the sheep of]

Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** comes up suddenly from **the thicket of the Jordan** to attack sheep in their pasture, so the enemy will suddenly attack Edom. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will attack suddenly, as a lion comes up from the thicket of the Jordan]
The pronoun **he** refers to the enemy whom Yahweh will send to attack Edom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the enemy will come up]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Edom were **the pastureland** where sheep graze safely. The word **continual** indicates that this pasture always has grass and water, so it means that Edom seemed to be a land that would always be secure. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land of Edom, which seemed always secure]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he will appoint whomever he chooses to rule over Edom. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And I will appoint over her whomever I choose!]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no one is like him and that no one can challenge him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For no one is like me, and no one will summon me!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if someone could **summon** him to a court of law to challenge what he does. It means that no one can challenge or oppose him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and who can oppose what I do]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a ruler as if he were a **shepherd**. It means that the ruler leads and protects his people as a shepherd leads and protects his sheep.
